Testimony of Becca Matusovich, Executive Director Children's Oral Health Network of Maine
LD 1746: An Act to Reduce Dental Disease and Ensure Access to Essential Preventive Dental Care Among Maine Children
Before the Committee on Health and Human Services Public Hearing: May 6, 2025
Good afternoon Representative Meyer, Senator lngwersen, and esteemed members of the Committee
on Health and Human Services. My name is Becca Matusovich and I am the Executive Director of the
Children's Oral Health Network of Maine, a statewide multi-sector network of organizations and individuals dedicated to ensuring that all children in Maine can grow up free from preventable dental
disease. I am excited to be here to ask you to support LD 1746.
As you heard from Rep. Gramlich, this bill includes both positions and programmatic components. The
two positions named in the bill are the same two time-limited positions we have been trying to save at the Maine CDC for the last few years. The governor included these two positions in her proposed
2026-27 biennial budget and this Committee already voted unanimously to support them earlier this
session. For that we are very grateful as it demonstrated your understanding and agreement of why
these positions are so essential to ensuring that children and families have access to preventive oral health care. Extending these two time-limited positions has been one of our top priorities in order to
ensure that Maine CDC can provide the important public health leadership that is needed to address
our state's oral health needs.
LD 1746 also includes some programmatic work that is needed from Maine CDC. As you already know, Maine is facing a significant oral health crisis, leaving about 2/3 of our kids without access to routine preventive dental care. There are almost 100,000 children with MaineCare who are not able to get even one checkup and cleaning a year.
To illustrate how this plays out in communities across Maine, I ask you to think of a teacher or a primary care provider who you know from your own district. Now imagine you are in their shoes today
rather than here - with 25 kids in your classroom, or with 25 kids scheduled in your office today.
Based on data from claims and the School Oral Health Program, we can estimate what oral health
access looks like for your 25 kids. If your classroom or patient panel is average for the state, you can
assume that only about 8 of your kids are getting annual checkups and cleanings. Among the rest, 14
will struggle to get an appointment because they have MaineCare, no dental insurance or have recently gotten coverage. This is especially heartbreaking because 5 of your kids already have active untreated decay and one needs an urgent referral to a dentist. This bill does not pretend to be the
entire solution but it offers a sensible low-cost strategy to slow down the cycle of dental disease for
the kids in your community.

Children's Oral Health Network I Becca Matusovich I becca@mainecohn.org I www.mainecohn.org

bear that cost in the form of pain and suffering, and a lifetime of poor health. We intentionally outlined the programmatic provisions in this bill to be flexible knowing that these are hard times. We know
from our experience with the pilots that informed this proposal that you can have a meaningful impact even starting with a very small investment in the first year, and a small infusion of state funds would help leverage more non-state resources. l have financial estimates from grant-funded pilot projects that I would be happy to share to help inform a fiscal note.
To wrap up, I will leave you with some of the questions that keep me up at night: > Back to the teacher or primary care provider you were thinking of - what do you think will

> What if there was an effective way to stop those cavities right in your building, today, with help
from programs that already exist and are already working on this? (you will hear from others
about how this can work!) > What if that kid with the urgent problem doesn't get help, what will happen to that child when
it erupts into an infection?
> Now zoom back out from your classroom or exam room to the statewide picture - your group of
25 kids is one of 10,000 classrooms and doctors offices, spread out all around the state. And if
screenings could be done in all ofthem today for the kids who haven't seen a dentist in the past
year, you would find more than 50,000 kids with untreated decay and close to 10,000 of them would need immediate referral.
Others are speaking today more specifically about how the two programmatic pieces of this bill can help schools and primary care providers deal with this challenge - to try to slow down the decay and
keep those 4 other kids with the untreated cavities from ending up in the ED, where the child with the urgent need is headed if someone doesn't intervene. Bigger solutions are obviously needed to build
out a dental workforce that can serve our state's whole population, and we all know those solutions will cost more and will take longer... but in the meantime if we don't do something to stop the decay that's already out there, then we are simply kicking the can over to the Emergency Room, and leaving kids in every community across this state to suffer from a disease that we have the tools to prevent
and to treat.
We have collaborated with many partners to bring you this practical and affordable action step to
make progress on a crisis that we know all of you want to solve. Please keep moving in the right
direction, and do all that is within your power to get LD 1746 enacted and funded.

State of Maine | 132nd Legislature Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services Testimony of Dr. Christopher Pezzullo on behalf of Maine Primary Care Association
May 6, 2025
Supporting: LD 1746, "An Act to Reduce Dental Disease and Ensure Access to Essential
Preventive Dental Care Among Maine Children" Sponsored by Representative Gramlich
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, I am Dr. Christopher Pezzullo, Chief Clinical Officer at Maine Primary Care Association (MPCA), and a pediatrician from Portland.
MPCA is a membership organization that represents Maine's Community Health Centers (CHCs), also known as Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs). Maine's CHCs make up the largest independent primary care network in the state, providing high quality and accessible primary and preventive medical, behavioral, and dental health services for over 200,000 people (1 in 6 Mainers) at more than 100 service delivery sites in all 16 Maine counties.
I strongly support LD 1746 and thank Representative Gramlich and other co-sponsors for bringing this legislation forward. This bill takes important steps to stop dental disease early and expand access to preventive care, strengthening Maine's overall public oral health infrastructure, particularly for Maine children.
In Maine, dental disease is the most common chronic disease in children, affecting their overall health, well-being, and school performance. During the 2023-24 school year, the School Oral Health Program visited over 200 schools and administered oral health screenings to more than 13,000 students. Of those screened, 30% had untreated decay, nearly 27% needed early intervention, and 6.5% needed immediate intervention. As a pediatrician, I support efforts to equip primary care providers with the ability to apply Silver Diamine Fluoride (SDF), a proven, effective treatment for arresting tooth decay.
This is practical step for the state to take to ensure that children receive the quality and accessible care they deserve. There is currently a shortage of oral health providers in Maine. Many CHCs, often one of the few providers in their service areas willing to accept MaineCare, have shared that they have waitlists of 100s. Primary care providers are poised to fill the void in oral health care by offering brief oral health screenings, fluoride varnish and SDF application. SDF is easily applied and can both halt and reverse dental cavities. It can also prevent the need for expensive and traumatic drilling and filling procedures.
I also support efforts to streamline the reimbursement of the application and ensure that it is offered by all insurers in Maine. SDF treatment can be rapidly taught to Maine's PCPs and provide a simple, low-cost treatment to a vexing public healthcare problem--how to provide care for dental disease in a state without access to oral health providers.
On behalf of Maine's Community Health Centers, thank you for considering my comments. Please do not hesitate to contact me directly at cpezzullo@mepca.org with any follow-up questions.
Dr. Christopher Pezzullo Chief Clinical Officer Maine Primary Care Association

May 6th, 2025
Dear Members of the Health and Human Services Committee:
My name is Jenna MacDonald, and I am writing testimony in support of LD1746-- An Act to Reduce Dental Disease and Ensure Access to Essential Preventive Dental Care Among Maine Children.
The Maine CDC School Oral Health Program provided 13,200 oral health screenings to students in over 229 Maine schools in the 2023-24 school year; 30% of the children screened had visible tooth decay. The number is likely higher because it doesn't take into account decay between teeth that may only be visible with imaging. As a dental hygienist practicing in School-Based Health Centers, I bear witness to the positive impact these dental programs have on Maine youth and would like to explain how this model improves health outcomes and dental access for our children.
Our federally qualified health center, Greater Portland Health, serves 34 schools throughout Cumberland County. Our dental hygienists, with mobile equipment in tow, commute to each of these schools to provide students with screenings and cleanings onsite so that parents do not need to miss work or other commitments in order for their children to get high-quality dental services. Our hygienists can determine which children have urgent or chronic needs and then work with school staff and parents to coordinate exams and treatment with our dentists. We are often able to see children within a week if they have emergency needs or within a couple of months for non-urgent needs. This is particularly helpful for families who have struggled to find dental homes for their children since being seen by a hygienist at their school connects them directly to one of our dentists. Close partnerships with school nurses allow our hygienists to coordinate getting parental permission to address care needs for specific students' challenges as well; oftentimes, we hear of individual students' dental problems from school nurses because a child's pain or discomfort is affecting their ability to learn, play or eat.
One patient story I have that stays vivid in my mind happened this year because we were able to expand to a new district with our partnerships with SOHP and COHN. One of the nurses reached out to me regarding a student experiencing dental pain and needed to be seen as soon as possible. I was able to squeeze the patient into the schedule the next day with our dentist. The patient had a severe infection that needed antibiotics first and then an extraction a week later. I was able to coordinate appointments needed with the student through WhatsApp, the school nurse and arranged transportation for multiple appointments, some of which they used public transportation and one we used Uber Health. All of this would not have been possible without our partnerships. The patient was also seen during our mobile hygiene clinic for preventative services.
Since the school year began, our school-based hygienists have been able to help coordinate exams with our dentists for hundreds of children who didn't have dental homes and have seen many more for routine or initial care. I cannot tell you how many times parents were unaware they had options since many offices in Maine do not provide care to MaineCare patients. Providing the opportunity for all schools to partner with dental professionals to facilitate access and help address needs appropriately is an incredibly effective first step in addressing the dental needs of Maine children. Since it is difficult to incentivize private dental practices to participate in caring for those insured with Medicaid, I would argue that the expansion of school-based programs and of existing clinics whose missions already support this population is the best way to meet this need.
Jenna MacDonald, MS, RDH Dental Practice Manager Greater Portland Health

Testimony in Support of LD 1746: An Act to Reduce Dental Disease and Ensure Access to Essential Preventive Dental Care Among Maine Children
5/5/2025
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and honorable members of the Health and Human Services Committee:
My name is Dr. Kailee Jorgenson, DMD, and I serve as the Clinical Director of Mainely Teeth and President of the Maine Oral Health Centers Alliance. I am writing to express my strong support for LD 1746, sponsored by Representative Lori Gramlich.
Dental disease remains the most common chronic condition among children, yet access to routine and preventive care is out of reach for far too many Maine families. Even among children with insurance, 65% do not receive regular dental care or have a dental home--this is a clear indicator that our current system is not meeting the needs of our youngest residents.
LD 1746 presents immediate, impactful solutions to this growing problem while easing the strain on Maine's already overextended dental workforce:
� Empowering primary care providers to apply Silver Diamine Fluoride and manage basic dental issues is a practical, evidence-based strategy. These providers often see children far more frequently than dentists, giving them a key opportunity to intervene early and prevent disease progression.
� Expanding mobile dental care through schools, modeled on successful local efforts, brings essential services directly to children in settings they already trust. With the right startup investment, this model can be scaled across the state and sustained through insurance reimbursement mechanisms.
� Preserving the Maine CDC's oral health infrastructure is essential. Without continued state-level coordination and support, these local programs cannot function effectively or reach the children who need care the most.
In addition to these solutions, I want to emphasize how challenging it is to manage the access-to-care crisis on the ground. The need is massive--not only for direct providers, but for those who can help coordinate care, assess needs, document what resources are lacking, and develop targeted, community-level interventions. We urgently need to increase the number of people involved in managing patients' dental needs, tracking outcomes, and planning long-term strategies to ensure every Maine child has access to preventive and therapeutic care. Without this kind of support, even well-designed care models will struggle to reach their full potential.

LD 1746 is a targeted, cost-effective step toward a stronger and more equitable oral health system. It leverages what we already know works, strengthens partnerships between health and education systems, and takes meaningful action to close persistent gaps in care.
I respectfully urge the Committee to vote Ought to Pass on LD 1746. This bill will make a real difference in the lives of Maine children and is a vital step toward a more sustainable, community-centered dental care system.
Thank you for your time, your service, and your commitment to improving oral health access for Maine's children.
Sincerely, Dr. Kailee Jorgenson, DMD Clinical Director, Mainely Teeth President, Maine Oral Health Centers Alliance

Kailee Jorgenson Augusta LD 1746

LD 1746: An Act to Reduce Dental Disease and Ensure Access to Essential Preventive Dental Care Among Maine Children
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and esteemed members of the Health and Human Services Committee,
My name is Lyvia Gaewsky, and I am the Program Manager of the From the First Tooth program--a statewide children's oral health initiative. Our program works to integrate oral health into primary care by providing technical assistance and training on how to perform an oral health risk assessment, evaluation, deliver parent and caregiver education, apply fluoride varnish, and more recently, how to apply silver diamine fluoride. I am writing to express our strong support for LD 1746, which takes critical steps to reduce dental disease and ensure that all Maine children--regardless of where they live or their insurance status--have access to preventive dental care.
LD 1746 offers evidence-based solutions that expand oral health access through primary care and the School Oral Health Program. Primary care is often a child's first and most consistent connection to the healthcare system, especially in the early years when dental visits are rare. Research and experience from programs like From the First Tooth show this approach works: families trust their primary care teams, providers are eager to expand their role in oral health, and young children can be reached early--before problems escalate. This strategy also helps ease the burden on Maine's already stretched dental workforce.
LD1746 would equip primary care providers with education and training on how to apply medically approved cavity-arresting treatments like silver diamine fluoride (SDF), which can stop cavity progression in its tracks before it turns into a painful and costly infection.
In spring of 2024 From the First Tooth partnered with two MaineHealth primary care practices to pilot SDF integration into primary care. Through the pilot, From the First Tooth successfully set up procedures, workflows, and provided training within the practices. Dear Members of the Health and Human Services Committee:
My name is Dr. Kristen Hoglund, and I am writing testimony in support of LD1746-- An Act to Reduce Dental Disease and Ensure Access to Essential Preventive Dental Care Among Maine Children.
The Maine CDC School Oral Health Program provided 13,200 oral health screenings to students in over 229 Maine schools in the 2023-24 school year; 30% of the children screened had visible tooth decay. The number is likely higher because it doesn't take into account decay between teeth that may only be visible with imaging. As a dentist practicing in School-Based Health Centers, I bear witness to the positive impact these dental programs have on Maine youth and would like to explain how this model improves health outcomes and dental access for our children.
Our federally qualified health center, Greater Portland Health, serves 34 schools throughout Cumberland County. Our dental hygienists, with mobile equipment in tow, commute to each of these schools to provide students with screenings and cleanings onsite so that parents do not need to miss work or other commitments in order for their children to get high-quality dental services. Our hygienists can determine which children have urgent or chronic needs and then work with school staff and parents to coordinate exams and treatment with our dentists. We are often able to see children within a week if they have emergency needs or within a couple of months for non-urgent needs. This is particularly helpful for families who have struggled to find dental homes for their children since being seen by a hygienist at their school connects them directly to one of our dentists. Close partnerships with school nurses allow our hygienists to coordinate getting parental permission to address care needs for specific students' challenges as well; oftentimes, we hear of individual students' dental problems from school nurses because a child's pain or discomfort is affecting their ability to learn, play or eat.
Children are generally resilient and tough, but many of our youth are suffering greatly with chronic dental pain and don't realize that it doesn't have to be this way. Only once their dental disease is managed do they realize what it means to have the quality of life that comes with a healthy mouth void of chronic pain. I will not forget the many times I have had kids come to me sad and suffering because they have not slept and cannot eat. Our team can provide treatment and be rewarded with smiling, vibrant and healthy kids at future visits. I cannot tell you how many children have cried while thanking and hugging me after I have removed teeth because they are so relieved that the suffering is over. It is heartbreaking but fulfilling to be able to reach children who may never have found dental treatment if not for our hygienists being active in schools.
Since the school year began, our school-based hygienists have been able to help coordinate exams with our dentists for hundreds of children who didn't have dental homes and have seen many more for routine or initial care. I cannot tell you how many times parents were unaware they had options since many offices in Maine do not provide care to MaineCare patients. Providing the opportunity for all schools to partner with dental professionals to facilitate access and help address needs appropriately is an incredibly effective first step in addressing the dental needs of Maine children. Since it is difficult to incentivize private dental practices to participate in caring for those insured with Medicaid, I would argue that the expansion of school-based programs and of existing clinics whose missions already support this population is the best way to meet this need.
Kristen Hoglund, DMD Dental Clinical Manager Greater Portland Health

Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services May 6, 2025
Good morning, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services. My name is Morgan Hynd, and I am the Director of the Bingham Program, a charitable endowment held at Tufts' Medical Center, established in 1932 to promote health and advance medicine in Maine. I am here to speak in support of LD 1746.
In addition to my role at the Bingham Program, I am also a Board member of the Children's Oral Health Network of Maine, and a long-standing member of the Maine Oral Health Funders, a philanthropic group dedicated to improving oral health. For more than two decades, philanthropy has done its best to fill in the gaps where state capacity has been limited, supporting community-based programs, workforce development, and prevention initiatives to ensure that children and families have access to the care they need. While these investments have made a meaningful impact, they can't possibly replace essential public health infrastructure that the state can provide.
Maine CDC data from the School Oral Health Program show that during the 2023-24 school year, 33% of the children seen through the program had some form of untreated dental decay. That's one out of every three children they saw during that year. The investments outlined in LD 1746 will ensure significant progress is made to reduce that number, resulting in healthier kids who are ready to learn in school and have better long-term health outcomes overall.
I was encouraged to see Governor Mills include two Maine CDC oral health positions in the biennial budget--this is a critical first step toward rebuilding the infrastructure Maine needs to sustain progress in oral health. With LD 1746, this Committee has an opportunity to go a few steps further by supporting enhanced school-based preventive oral health services, more capacity for the system through support of mobile dental services, and critical training and education that will allow primary care providers to catch and treat dental disease in young children as early as possible. Philanthropy has helped to jumpstart real progress by investing in these areas, but lasting change needs more than just early momentum. State support would be a turbo boost-- amplifying what's already working, expanding our reach, and ensuring these gains aren't just initiated, but sustained.

The philanthropic community deeply values its partnership with the state and we hope to continue to grow this public/private partnership through strategic efforts like those outlined in LD 1746. I urge this Committee to build on its legacy of bipartisan support for better oral health for Maine children. Your vote in support of LD 1746 is essential to keeping Maine children healthy and ready to thrive. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Morgan Hynd Warren LD 1746

Teresa Alley Jonesport LD 1746
Testimony of Teresa Alley, Oral Health Coordinator, Washington County Children's Program for LD 1746: An Act to Reduce Dental Disease and Ensure Access to Essential Preventive Dental Care Among Maine Children Before the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee and the Health and Human Services Committee Public Hearing: May 6, 2025 Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Health and Human Services Committee, my name is Teresa Alley, I am a dental hygienist, and I reside in Jonesport. I am in favor of LD 1746 due to the positive impacts it will have for Maine's children. Since 1999, I have administered the CDC School Oral Health Program in Washington County and have served almost 1000 students each year enrolled at Washington County elementary schools. In my vast experience, children living in Washington County are experiencing the greatest barrier to oral health services than ever before. The community health centers, who serve the largest number of individuals enrolled in MaineCare, regularly don't have dental providers to care for our residents. Several of the health centers are experiencing a nine-month waiting period to see a dental provider. Personally, I know too many children who go to bed each night with tooth aches. It is common for children to tell me they are unable to go to the dentist and that their parents know they are in pain. Recently one such child said "Mom will take me to the dentist after we have our roof fixed." Frequently children report they do not have their own toothbrush or toothpaste. Only the lucky child can access restorative care when our school-based preventive measures are not enough to help children who suffer from unsightly, painful decayed teeth. Dental disease affects the child's ability to speak, their self-esteem, and ability to concentrate and learn while in school. I continue to observe the positive impacts the school-based oral health program has for our County. Families in our County have come to depend on our services, and we are often the only dental provider who will care for them the strength of our program is that we serve children within the school, meaning parents do not have to take time off work or figure out transportation to ensure children get care. By supporting comprehensive mobile dental care in coordination with the CDC School Oral Health Program the decay rates for children throughout the State will also reduce. With the use of silver diamine fluoride (a cavity stopping treatment) and other preventive measures, the decay rate for children in our program reduced from 35% to as low as 23%. By empowering primary care providers to also apply silver diamine fluoride during well child visits, the number of children with dental disease will be reduced, especially since children are more likely to be able to get in to see a primary care doctor than a dentist. We rely deeply on the support we receive from the Maine Oral Health Program of the Maine CDC. Upon my arrival in the public health sector in 1999, the Maine Oral Health Program employed four staff members. Over time, that number dwindled to zero. It is crucial to restore the infrastructure at the State level. Additional staff will continue to offer technical support to oral health entities that serve Maine's most venerable residents: our children. Thank you for your consideration of my testimony on this important issue.

In order to ensure that ALL children, regardless of family economic status, receive at least one preventive dental visit annually it's absolutely essential the first two sections of this bill are passed and that the necessary funding is appropriated.
While we support most of the tenets in this bill, the MDA has concerns about Section 3 as it
relates to "minimally invasive dental disease treatment" . This often means silver diamine fluoride (SDF) and/or fluoride varnish. There has been strong research interest in the use of SDF to arrest caries lesions, which is an off-label use. SDF currently has the Food and Drug

of SDF treatment is permanent black staining of the arrested caries lesions. This means
children who receive SDF have visible black stains on their teeth that do not come off. The

10050233:
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and distinguished members of the Health and Human Services Committee,
My name is Traci Dempsey, I live in Bath, Maine. I president of the Maine Dental Hygienists' Association that represents the nearly 1300 licensed dental hygienists in Maine. We urge you to vote OTP on LD 1746.
Tooth decay is the most common chronic disease of childhood yet it is entirely preventable. Children with untreated dental problems are more likely to miss school, struggle to eat and sleep, and suffer longterm health consequences. This legislation recognizes that prevention and early intervention are key and it brings care directly to where children and families already are.
Specifically, this bill funds school-based dental care programs bringing preventive services like screenings, sealants, fluoride treatments, and cleanings to children in school. Although there is a cost to fund these programs they have been proven to improve oral health outcomes, reduce absenteeism, and lower long-term costs especially of emergency room visits for urgent dental needs.
This legislation also supports mobile dental services that reach rural, low-income, and otherwise hard-toreach communities. Mobile units help bridge the gap in access for families who face barriers like transportation, time off work, or lack of local providers.
Another part of this bill Invests in training primary care providers to incorporate basic oral health into their routine care. Pediatricians, family physicians, and nurse practitioners are often the first--and sometimes only--health professionals that young children see. Equipping them with the tools and knowledge to assess oral health and apply preventive measures like silver diamine fluoride greatly decreases progression decay buying time for children to be seen by a dentist and could keep them out of pain and infection.
This is a practical, equitable, and forward-thinking approach to oral health. By integrating dental care into schools, mobile services, and primary care settings, we can catch problems early, reduce disparities, and make oral health part of whole-person care.
I urge you to support this legislation. It is an investment in healthier children, stronger communities, and a more accessible oral care.
Thank you for your leadership and for your commitment to advancing oral health. I am happy to answer any questions.
Thank you,
Traci L. Dempsey, RDH, IPDH President, Maine Dental Hygienists' Association Resident of Bath, ME
10049205:
Strong Support for LD 1746: An Act to Reduce Dental Disease and Ensure Access to Essential Preventive Dental Care Among Maine Children
Dear Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Health and Human Services Committee,
My name is Melinda Nadeau, and I am a dedicated school nurse in Brunswick. I am here on Behalf of Maine Association of School Nurses and myself in my strongest support for LD 1746: An Act to Reduce Dental Disease and Ensure Access to Essential Preventive Dental Care Among Maine Children.
As a school nurse who has spent over a decade engaged with Maine's School Oral Health Program, I have seen firsthand the importance of bringing oral health services directly into the school setting. My support for LD 1746 is shaped by countless experiences with students whose lives were improved through timely dental interventions. That said, while school-based screenings and fluoride varnish programs are valuable, they are often not enough to address the comprehensive dental needs of many of our students.
Oral health greatly impacts the well-being of the students across schools in Maine. Beyond the obvious pain and discomfort, dental disease contributes to missed school days, difficulty concentrating in class, and even impacts their overall health and self-esteem. In one instance, an oral screening through our program even helped identify a child in renal failure. Unfortunately, once children are screened it can be challenging to connect them to further care if they are in need of it.
LD 1746 offers a crucial and innovative approach to tackling this crisis, building on models that we know work. Integrating silver diamine fluoride into the primary care setting makes perfect sense for early intervention and prevention, especially as dental providers are scarce. And, scaling up the school-based oral health care delivery model refined in Cumberland County would be a game-changer for our children's oral health. This model not only removes barriers like transportation and cost but also creates a familiar and trusted environment for care. The extra layer of supportive care coordination for children who require care from a dentist is an important component in an oral health delivery system that is inaccessible to the children I see who need it most.
The ability to sustain, coordinate, and replicate this work statewide, with support from a well-resourced Oral Health Program at the CDC, represents a long overdue investment in children's overall health, equity, and academic success.
As someone who has been advocating for children's oral health for more than a decade, I urge you to support LD 1746 and invest in the oral health of Maine's children. This bill represents a significant step forward in ensuring that all children have the opportunity for a healthy smile and a brighter future.
Thank you for your time and consideration of this critical legislation.
Sincerely,

Melinda Nadeau School Nurse
